questions.stem: What can we learn about the MH370 tragedy from the news report?
options: A) A lawsuit has been filed against Malaysia Airlines.
B) The missing passengers' bodies have been found.
C) The cause of the disappearance has been unveiled.
D) Flight MH370 got lost during its trip to Hong Kong.

explain.定位:
In Beijing, relatives of Chinese passengers on the missing flight have filed a lawsuit against
Malaysia Airlines.
在北京，失联航班上中国乘客的家属已经对马来西亚航空提起了诉讼。
explain.信号:
已完成动作的陈述句。这句用现在完成时 have filed a lawsuit against Malaysia Airlines
直陈一个已经发生的事实——家属已起诉航空公司，是报道里少数被明确坐实的进展，正好
对应选项 A，所以它是答案句。其余强陈述（找到遗体、查明原因）原文全程没坐实。
explain.替换:
relatives of Chinese passengers on the missing flight have filed a lawsuit against Malaysia Airlines
↔ A lawsuit has been filed against Malaysia Airlines.
主动转被动同一事
explain.排除:
B) 未提及
原文从头到尾没提到找到任何乘客遗体——被发现的是 a piece of debris（一块残骸），不
是人。The missing passengers' bodies have been found. 把“残骸”偷换成“遗体”，是凭
常识脑补出来的，原文无据。
C) 与原文相反
原文里专家只是 studying a piece of debris，且明说 If it's confirmed to be a piece of
the missing flight——连残骸身份都还没确认，更谈不上揭晓失联原因。The cause of the
disappearance has been unveiled. 把“还在研究、尚待确认”说成“原因已揭晓”，与原文的
未定状态相反。
借用原文：If it's confirmed to be a piece of the missing flight
D) 偷换概念
原文明说航班 vanished en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing——从吉隆坡飞往北京。
Flight MH370 got lost during its trip to Hong Kong. 盗用了“航班失联途中”这层意思，
却把目的地从 Beijing 偷改成 Hong Kong，是听到 got lost 就想选、却没核对地名的陷
阱。
借用原文：vanished en route from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing

questions.stem: Where was the first debris of the missing MH370 found?
options: A) On a beach in Mozambique.

explain.定位:
If it's confirmed to be a piece of the missing flight, it would be the second to be washed up on
a shore last year, a section of the plane's wing was found off Reunion Island.
如果它被确认是失联客机的残骸，那将是冲上岸的第二块；去年，飞机的一段机翼曾在留尼
汪岛附近被发现。
explain.信号:
second 反衬出 first 在哪。题干问 first（第一块），原文先说莫桑比克这块若确认将是
the second（第二块），紧接着才点出真正的第一块——a section of the plane's wing
was found off Reunion Island。是 second 这个序数词信号反衬出：留尼汪岛那次才是
first。听 where 题要抓住这种 first/second 的次序词来对号。
explain.替换:
a section of the plane's wing was found off Reunion Island ↔ In Reunion Island.
地名原样保留
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
莫桑比克确实在原文里出现——a piece of debris found last week on a beach in
Mozambique，但那是上周新发现、且若确认将是 the second 块。题干问的是 first，On
a beach in Mozambique. 盗用了刚念到的、印象最深的地名，却答非所问。
借用原文：a piece of debris found last week on a beach in Mozambique
B) 原词陷阱
原文里 Malaysia Airlines 反复出现，但那是航空公司名（马航），不是残骸发现地；马来
西亚只是航班始发国。In Malaysia. 把频繁听到的 Malaysia 一词错当成发现地点。
借用原文：Malaysia Airlines
D) 张冠李戴
In Beijing 在原文出现过，但说的是航班目的地、以及家属在北京起诉，与残骸发现地无
关。In Beijing. 盗用了这个地名，却挂错了事件。
借用原文：In Beijing, relatives of Chinese passengers on the missing flight have filed a lawsuit
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1 This is Lebanon. Nearly two million Syrian refugees have settled. As another harsh winter sets in,
many people struggle to keep their tents warm enough for their young children. About 195,000 Syrian
families are particularly at risk. The number of years that refugees have stayed here means that they are
facing increasing vulnerabilities. All of their savings have been depleted. Many have moved into the
settlements because they are cheaper than living in flats or apartments in town. They are not used to
these conditions. It is practically impossible to find a job and therefore they have no income and are
totally reliant on resources from humanitarian agencies. A snowstorm over the weekend worsened
conditions for many families. Some stayed inside huddled around their stoves to keep warm. One refugee
says, "It's important to keep my children alive. The cold is easier than death, barrel bombs and shelling."

questions.stem: Why did many refugees move into the settlements?
options: A) Because they are used to living here.
B) Because it is cheaper for them to live here.
C) Because it is easier for them to get a job.
D) Because the government forced them to live here.

explain.定位:
Many have moved into the settlements because they are cheaper than living in flats or
apartments in town.
许多人搬进了这些安置点，因为它们比住在城里的公寓或套房更便宜。
explain.信号:
because 引出原因。答案句靠一个明摆着的因果信号锁定：because they are cheaper
than living in flats or apartments in town 里的 because 直接引出“搬进来”的原因，
because 后面那半句就是答案落点。这与第一步“专候 because/cheaper”的预备完全
对上。
explain.替换:
cheaper than living in flats or apartments in town ↔ it is cheaper for them to live here
同义压缩
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
Because they are used to living here. 盗用了录音里的 They are not used to these
conditions. 中的 used to 来诱选：录音明说他们“不习惯”这些条件，选项却改成“住惯了”，
正好把原文的否定 not 抹掉、意思反转，听到 used to 就选必中陷阱。
借用原文：They are not used to these conditions.
C) 与原文相反
Because it is easier for them to get a job. 盗用了录音里的 job 来诱选：录音说的是 It is
practically impossible to find a job（几乎找不到工作），选项却说成“更容易找到工作”，
把“找不到”偷换成“好找”，与原文相反，听到 job 就选会落坑。
借用原文：It is practically impossible to find a job
D) 未提及
Because the government forced them to live here. 说是“政府强迫他们住这里”，但录音
通篇只讲他们因为便宜而“主动搬入”（Many have moved into the settlements because
they are cheaper），从未提到任何政府强制，属凭常识想当然添加的原因。

questions.stem: What made the conditions of settlements worse for the refugees?

explain.定位:
A snowstorm over the weekend worsened conditions for many families.
周末的一场暴风雪让许多家庭的处境更加恶化。
explain.信号:
worsened 点出结果。答案句靠“结果信号”锁定：A snowstorm over the weekend
worsened conditions for many families 里的 worsened（使……恶化）正对题干的
made…worse，紧挨这个结果词、作主语的 snowstorm 就是起因。听到“使条件变差”这层
意思，主语即答案。
explain.替换:
A snowstorm over the weekend worsened conditions ↔ The snowstorm.
原词即答案
explain.排除:
B) 张冠李戴
The bombing. 盗用了录音结尾难民引语里的 barrel bombs and shelling（桶装炸弹与炮
击）来诱选：但那是难民形容“冷比死亡、炸弹、炮击更易忍受”时提到的，是背景威胁，并
非“让安置点条件变糟”的那件事，把别处提到的轰炸安到本题起因上，张冠李戴。
借用原文：barrel bombs and shelling
C) 未提及
The war. 借战乱大背景诱选：全文讲的是叙利亚难民因战乱外逃，war 是隐含背景，但录音
从没说“战争让安置点条件变糟”，真正点名导致恶化的是 A snowstorm over the weekend
worsened conditions。听到难民题就想当然选 war 会落坑。
D) 未提及
The starvation. 说是“饥饿”让条件变糟，但录音只提到 they have no income（没有收
入），从未出现 starvation/饥饿，也没把任何挨饿与“条件恶化”挂钩，属由“难民→缺粮”的
常识脑补。

questions.stem: What's the purpose of launching McChoco Potato?

explain.定位:
The chocolate fries are McDonald's Japan's attempt to reverse poor sales.
这款巧克力薯条是麦当劳日本公司为扭转低迷销量所做的尝试。
explain.信号:
attempt to 点出意图。attempt to reverse poor sales 里的 attempt to（试图、尝试
去）是典型的『目的信号』，它后面跟的 reverse poor sales（扭转糟糕的销量）就是推出
这款薯条的真正目的，这一句就是答案句。
explain.替换:
reverse poor sales ↔ Improving customer sales.
扭转差销量＝提升销量，反义+否定转换
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
录音开头确实说把巧克力薯条 adding French fries with chocolate sauce to its menu，A
项 Enriching the menu. 就盗用了 menu 这个词，但『加进菜单』只是动作本身，不是这
么做的目的，目的句明确是扭转销量。听到 menu 就选 A 正中陷阱。
借用原文：adding French fries with chocolate sauce to its menu
B) 原词陷阱
录音后文说 The chocolate fries have been extremely popular with customers，B 项
Meeting customer needs. 借 customers 一词制造『满足顾客需求』的错觉，但那是产品
上市后的反响，不是当初推出它的目的，目的句只谈销量。
借用原文：extremely popular with customers
C) 与原文相反
录音明说 McDonald's Japan closed hundreds of the restaurants，是大量关店，C 项
Opening new branches. 恰好说反成『开新店』，与原文方向相反，且和推薯条的目的无
关。
借用原文：McDonald's Japan closed hundreds of the restaurants

questions.stem: Who is Sarah Casanova?

explain.定位:
"Undoubtedly, 2015 was the most challenging year we have faced in our 45-year history,"
said McDonald's Japan's president Sarah Casanova.
麦当劳日本公司总裁莎拉·卡萨诺瓦说：『毫无疑问，2015 年是我们 45 年历史上最艰难的
一年。』
explain.信号:
人名紧贴头衔同位语。录音用 said McDonald's Japan's president Sarah Casanova 把头
衔和人名连在一起说出来，president 紧贴 Sarah Casanova，这种『头衔+人名』的同位结
构就是介绍身份的答案信号。
explain.替换:
McDonald's Japan's president Sarah Casanova ↔ McDonald's Japan's president.
头衔几乎原样对应
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
录音里 U.S.-based 是用来修饰开店的那家美国母公司 U.S.-based McDonald's opened its
first restaurant，A 项 U.S.-based McDonald's president. 盗用 U.S.-based 拼到
president 上，但 Casanova 的头衔明明是 Japan's president，国别听错就掉坑。
借用原文：U.S.-based McDonald's opened its first restaurant in Tokyo
B) 原词陷阱
录音确有 customers 一词 popular with customers，B 项 McDonald's Japan's
customer. 借它把 Casanova 说成顾客，但她被明确介绍为 president（总裁），身份不
符。
借用原文：popular with customers
D) 原词陷阱
D 项 U.S.-based McDonald's customer. 同时拼凑录音里出现过的 U.S.-based 和
customer 两个词，但 Casanova 既不是美国方、也不是顾客，是把两处原词各偷一个胡乱
组合，国别和身份全错。
借用原文：U.S.-based McDonald's opened its first restaurant in Tokyo

questions.stem: When was the first McDonald's restaurant opened up in Tokyo?

explain.定位:
U.S.-based McDonald's opened its first restaurant in Tokyo in 1971.
美国麦当劳于 1971 年在东京开设了第一家餐厅。
explain.信号:
事件词 first restaurant 配年份。题目问 first restaurant 开业时间，录音里把 opened its
first restaurant in Tokyo in 1971 这件事和年份 1971 直接绑在一起，事件词（first
restaurant、Tokyo）和年份同句出现，就是答案信号。
explain.替换:
opened its first restaurant in Tokyo in 1971 ↔ In 1971.
年份数字原样对应
explain.排除:
D) 原词陷阱
录音里 2015 was the most challenging year 的 2015 是说明那年生意最艰难，D 项 In
2015. 盗用这个显眼的近年数字，但它对应的事件是『最艰难的一年』，不是开店，张冠李
戴。
借用原文：2015 was the most challenging year we have faced
B) 未提及
B 项 In 1991. 在录音中根本没被念到，它只是和真年份 1971 读音相近，用来干扰没记清数
字、靠耳朵蒙的人。
C) 未提及

When I was working full-time as a salesman for a big company，When I was… 把时

questions.stem: What has the speaker learned from his friendship with Joe?

questions.stem: Cooking benefits people in many ways and enables them to connect with one another.
questions.passage:
How to Eat Well

A) Why do so many Americans eat tons of processed food, the stuff that is correctly called junk(垃圾) and should really carry warning labels?

B) It's not because fresh ingredients are hard to come by. Supermarkets offer more variety than ever, and there are over four times as many farmers' markets in the U.S. as there were 20 years ago. Nor is it for lack of available information. There are plenty of recipes(食谱) how-to videos and cooking classes available to anyone who has a computer, smartphone or television. If anything, the information is overwhelming.

C) And yet we aren't cooking. If you eat three meals a day and behave like most Americans, you probably get at least a third of your daily calories(卡路里) outside the home. Nearly two thirds of us grab fast food once a week, and we get almost 25% of our daily calories from snacks. So we're eating out or taking in, and we don't sit down—or we do, but we hurry.

D) Shouldn't preparing—and consuming—food be a source of comfort, pride, health, well-being, relaxation, sociability? Something that connects us to other humans? Why should we want to outsource(外包) this basic task, especially when outsourcing it is so harmful?

E) When I talk about cooking, I'm not talking about creating elaborate dinner parties or three-day science projects. I'm talking about simple, easy, everyday meals. My mission is to encourage green hands and those lacking time or money to feed themselves. That means we need modest, realistic expectations, and we need to teach people to cook food that's good enough to share with family and friends.

F) Perhaps a return to real cooking needn't be far off. A recent Harris poll revealed that 79% of Americans say they enjoy cooking and 30% "love it"; 14% admit to not enjoying kitchen work and just 7% won't go near the stove at all. But this doesn't necessarily translate to real cooking, and the result of this survey shouldn't surprise anyone: 52% of those 65 or older cook at home five or more times per week; only a third of young people do.

G) Back in the 1950s most of us grew up in households where Mom cooked virtually every night. The intention to put a home-cooked meal on the table was pretty much universal. Most people couldn't afford to do otherwise.

H) Although frozen dinners were invented in the 40s, their popularity didn't boom until televisions became popular a decade or so later. Since then, packaged, pre-prepared meals have been what's for dinner. The microwave and fast-food chains were the biggest catalyst(催化剂), but the big food companies—which want to sell anything except the raw ingredients that go into cooking—made the home cook an endangered species.

questions.stem: What is happening to the wallet?
options: D) It is changing in style.
questions.passage:
The wallet is heading for extinction. As a day-to-day essential, it will die off with the generation who read print newspapers. The kind of shopping—where you hand over notes and count out change in return—now happens only in the most minor of our retail encounters, like buying a bar of chocolate or a pint of milk from a corner shop. At the shops where you spend any real money, that money is increasingly abstracted. And this is more and more true, the higher up the scale you go. At the most cutting-edge retail stores—Victoria Beckham on Dover Street, for instance—you don't go and stand at any kind of cash register when you decide to pay. The staff are equipped with iPads to take your payment while you relax on a sofa.

Which is nothing more or less than excellent service, if you have the money. But across society, the abstraction of the idea of cash makes me uneasy. Maybe I'm just old-fashioned. But earning money isn't quick or easy for most of us. Isn't it a bit weird that spending it should happen in half a blink(眨眼) of an eye? Doesn't a wallet—that time-honoured Friday-night feeling of pleasing, promising fatness—represent something that matters?

But I'll leave the economics to the experts. What bothers me about the death of the wallet is the change it represents in our physical environment. Everything about the look and feel of a wallet—the way the fastenings and materials wear and tear and loosen with age, the plastic and paper and gold and silver, and handwritten phone numbers and printed cinema tickets—is the very opposite of what our world is becoming. The opposite of a wallet is a smartphone or an iPad. The rounded edges, cool glass, smooth and unknowable as a pebble(鹅卵石). Instead of digging through pieces of paper and peering into corners, we move our fingers left and right. No more counting out coins. Show your wallet, if you still have one. It may not be here much longer.

questions.stem: What does the author say about people's sleeping habits?
options: C) They change with the seasons.
D) They vary from person to person.
questions.passage:
Everybody sleeps, but what people stay up late to catch—or wake up early in order not to miss—varies by culture.

From data collected, it seems the things that cause us to lose the most sleep, on average, are sporting events, time changes, and holidays.

Around the world, people changed sleep patterns thanks to the start or end of daylight savings time. Russians, for example, began to wake up about a half-hour later each day after President Vladimir Putin shifted the country permanently to "winter time" starting on October 26.

Russia's other late nights and early mornings generally correspond to public holidays. On New Year's Eve, Russians have the world's latest bedtime, hitting the hay at around 3:30 a.m.

Russians also get up an hour later on International Women's Day, the day for treating and celebrating female relatives.

Similarly, Americans' late nights, late mornings, and longest sleeps fall on three-day weekends. Canada got the least sleep of the year the night it beat Sweden in the Olympic hockey(冰球). The World Cup is also chiefly responsible for sleep deprivation(剥夺). The worst night for sleep in the U.K was the night of the England-Italy match on June 14. Brits stayed up a half-hour later to watch it, and then they woke up earlier than usual the next morning thanks to summer nights, the phenomenon in which the sun barely sets in northern countries in the summertime. That was nothing, though, compared to Germans, Italians, and the French, who stayed up around an hour and a half later on various days throughout the summer to watch the Cup.

It should be made clear that not everyone has a device to record their sleep patterns; in some of these nations, it's likely that only the richest people do. And people who elect to track their sleep may try to get more sleep than the average person. Even if that's the case, though, the above findings are still striking. If the most health-conscious among us have such deep swings in our shut-eye levels throughout the year, how much sleep are the rest of us losing?

questions.stem: What is the major cause for Europeans' loss of sleep?
questions.passage:
Everybody sleeps, but what people stay up late to catch—or wake up early in order not to miss—varies by culture.

From data collected, it seems the things that cause us to lose the most sleep, on average, are sporting events, time changes, and holidays.

Around the world, people changed sleep patterns thanks to the start or end of daylight savings time. Russians, for example, began to wake up about a half-hour later each day after President Vladimir Putin shifted the country permanently to "winter time" starting on October 26.

Russia's other late nights and early mornings generally correspond to public holidays. On New Year's Eve, Russians have the world's latest bedtime, hitting the hay at around 3:30 a.m.

Russians also get up an hour later on International Women's Day, the day for treating and celebrating female relatives.

Similarly, Americans' late nights, late mornings, and longest sleeps fall on three-day weekends. Canada got the least sleep of the year the night it beat Sweden in the Olympic hockey(冰球). The World Cup is also chiefly responsible for sleep deprivation(剥夺). The worst night for sleep in the U.K was the night of the England-Italy match on June 14. Brits stayed up a half-hour later to watch it, and then they woke up earlier than usual the next morning thanks to summer nights, the phenomenon in which the sun barely sets in northern countries in the summertime. That was nothing, though, compared to Germans, Italians, and the French, who stayed up around an hour and a half later on various days throughout the summer to watch the Cup.

It should be made clear that not everyone has a device to record their sleep patterns; in some of these nations, it's likely that only the richest people do. And people who elect to track their sleep may try to get more sleep than the average person. Even if that's the case, though, the above findings are still striking. If the most health-conscious among us have such deep swings in our shut-eye levels throughout the year, how much sleep are the rest of us losing?

writing.directions: Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay commenting on the saying “Never go out there to see what happens, go out there to make things happen.” You can cite examples to illustrate the importance of being participants rather than mere onlookers in life. You should write at least 120 words but no more than 180 words.
writing.model:
The saying "Never go out there to see what happens, go out there to make things happen" urges us to be active
creators of our own lives rather than passive bystanders. In my view, this attitude is exactly what turns dreams
into reality, and I firmly stand with those who choose to make things happen.
Those who merely stand by and watch often let precious opportunities slip away. Take Jack Ma as an example.
When most people were still doubting the Internet, he took the initiative to start Alibaba, seizing the chance
that others were only observing. Had he chosen to be a mere onlooker, China's e-commerce might never
have flourished as it does today. His story shows that only by stepping forward and acting can we shape
the outcome.
Therefore, we should never wait on the sidelines for good things to appear. Instead, let us take the initiative,
seize every opportunity, and become participants who make things happen.

translation.reference: The annual Chinese language speaking contest for foreigners was held in Changsha this year. The contest has proved to be a good way to promote cultural exchanges between China and the rest of the world. It offered young people around the world an opportunity to better understand China. A total of 126 contestants from 87 countries gathered in the capital of Hunan Province to take part in the semifinals and finals held from July 6 to August 5. The contest was not the only activity.
